name: Madhya Pradesh
tagline: Where the unfinished still feels eternal
intro: Madhya Pradesh is often described through its great historical cities, ancient dynasties, forests, rivers and celebrated monuments. But beyond the places that appear most often in travel conversations lies another Madhya Pradesh — one made of quiet hills, riverbanks, caves, unfinished shrines, village deities and temples where faith has remained deeply woven into everyday life. Some of these sacred places are architecturally extraordinary. Others are humble, almost hidden from the outside world. What connects them is not grandeur, but the feeling that they were created around a particular relationship between the divine and the landscape.

In these temples, Shiva is found inside rock, beside rivers, beneath enormous stone roofs and in forms that seem to emerge directly from nature. The Goddess appears on forested hills, as a protector of communities and as a presence approached through the physical act of climbing. Yogini shrines open themselves to the sky, while Jain pilgrimage landscapes rise into the Satpura and Vindhya country with an atmosphere of stillness and renunciation. Even the unfinished temples have a strange spiritual power: they remind us that sacredness does not always depend on completion.

This is an exploration of ten such places. They are not presented simply as monuments to visit, but as sacred landscapes to understand — places where legend, devotion, memory and nature continue to meet.

temples.name: Bhojeshwar Temple
temples.essence: Where the Unfinished Still Feels Eternal

body.p: There is something deeply moving about entering Bhojeshwar Temple. The temple is incomplete, yet the first impression is not one of absence. It is one of immense presence. At its heart stands a colossal Shiva lingam carved from a single stone, rising with a scale that makes the human body suddenly feel very small. The temple was begun in the eleventh century under the Paramara ruler Raja Bhoja and was never completed, but generations have continued to worship Shiva here. The unfinished structure therefore does not feel abandoned. It feels as though the prayer continued even after the builders stopped.

The spiritual experience of Bhojpur comes from this contrast. The massive stones, the unfinished architectural plans and the extraordinary lingam create a sense of a sacred intention that outlived the original project. Devotees do not need the temple to be architecturally complete for the sanctum to feel complete in another sense. Shiva is already present. The unfinished walls become part of the story: human beings may begin with a vision, but the divine does not wait for every human detail to be resolved before becoming sacred.

Bhojeshwar is especially powerful for those who are carrying something unfinished in their own lives. A dream that has taken longer than expected. A relationship that changed before it reached the ending one imagined. A chapter that remains unresolved. The temple seems to quietly say that incompleteness is not always failure. Sometimes what remains unfinished can still hold enormous meaning.

Surrounded by the hills and the landscape of the Betwa, Bhojpur feels less like a conventional temple complex and more like a conversation between stone, sky and devotion. People come to offer prayers to Shiva, particularly on auspicious occasions, but many leave with something more inward: the feeling that a sacred life does not have to be a perfectly finished life.

temples.name: Chausath Yogini Temple
temples.essence: Where the Sacred Circle Holds the Sky

body.p: On a hill above the plains of Morena stands one of Madhya Pradesh's most unusual sacred spaces: the circular Chausath Yogini Temple at Mitawali. Unlike the conventional temple image of a straight entrance leading toward a single sanctum, this shrine unfolds as a circle. Its ring of chambers was dedicated to the Yoginis, powerful feminine manifestations associated with the Goddess, while the central sacred space is associated with Shiva. The entire form creates a feeling of a world enclosed within a circle, with the open sky becoming part of the temple itself.

The spiritual imagination behind a Yogini shrine is different from the more familiar idea of worshipping one deity in isolation. Here, divine feminine power is understood through multiplicity. The many Yoginis suggest that the sacred can appear through different energies, moods and forms. Protection, fertility, transformation, courage, knowledge, mystery and fierce power can all belong to the same divine reality. Standing within the circular enclosure, one can feel how different this is from simply looking at a statue. The architecture itself becomes a meditation on wholeness.

The hilltop setting adds another layer. The temple looks outward across the surrounding landscape while simultaneously turning inward toward its own sacred centre. Historically, the site is also associated with the study of astrology and mathematics, giving it an unusual relationship between cosmic order and sacred architecture. The circle, the sky and the movement of the sun seem to belong to the same symbolic language.

Perhaps this is why Mitawali feels less like a temple one merely enters and more like a space one enters into. It reminds us that the sacred does not always move in a straight line. Sometimes it circles back. Sometimes it surrounds us. Sometimes the centre is found only after we stop looking for a single direction.

temples.name: Chausath Yogini Temple
temples.essence: Where the Mother Watches Over the Narmada

body.p: Above the Narmada at Bhedaghat stands another extraordinary Yogini temple, circular in form and unusually rich in its representation of the feminine divine. Although popularly called a Chausath Yogini temple, the surviving circular enclosure contains 81 shrine spaces. The temple rises above the river landscape, creating an atmosphere in which the powerful movement of the Narmada below seems to meet the stillness of the stone circle above.

The spiritual significance of such a space lies in the idea of the Goddess not as one limited personality, but as a field of many powers. Yogini traditions are associated with fierce, mysterious and transformative aspects of feminine energy. These are not simply gentle representations of divinity. They belong to the deeper Indian understanding that creation and destruction, protection and transformation, beauty and fear can exist within the same cosmic reality.

For a devotee, the setting itself can become part of the prayer. The Narmada flows below, the sky opens above, and the circular temple holds its many sacred presences around the devotee. The movement of the river and the stillness of the shrine create a natural rhythm: everything changes, yet something remains centred.

There is also a deeper emotional quality to the temple. The Goddess in her Yogini forms can be understood as a reminder that strength does not always look peaceful. Sometimes protection requires fierceness. Sometimes transformation feels uncomfortable before it becomes liberating. To stand in this temple is therefore to encounter a form of spirituality that does not ask us to deny the difficult parts of life, but to recognise that they too can belong to the sacred.

temples.name: Salkanpur Maa Vijayasana
temples.essence: The Goddess Who Is Reached One Step at a Time

body.p: High above the landscape of Sehore, on a hill associated with Maa Vijayasana or Beejasan Devi, the journey to the shrine becomes part of the act of worship. The temple stands on a hill about 800 feet high, and generations of devotees have approached the Goddess through a long climb. The physical ascent is simple, but spiritually it can feel like a conversation between effort and faith. Each step asks the devotee to continue.

The Goddess here is understood as a form of Durga, a protective and victorious presence. Local tradition connects her with the idea of triumph after struggle, and the name Vijayasana carries the feeling of victory and divine strength. People come seeking protection, fulfilment of wishes, courage and the blessings of the Mother. For many families, the shrine is not an occasional destination but part of an inherited relationship with the Goddess.

What makes Salkanpur powerful is the way devotion becomes physical. A prayer is no longer only something spoken with folded hands. It becomes breath, sweat, repetition and persistence. The hill does not allow the devotee to arrive instantly. It creates a small pilgrimage within the pilgrimage.

The landscape strengthens the feeling. As the hill rises away from the ordinary world below, the shrine gradually becomes less about the noise of daily life and more about the inward state of the person climbing. Some devotees climb with a specific wish. Others come in gratitude. Some carry the prayers of their families. And some simply come because they have been coming for years.
Salkanpur therefore represents a beautiful truth about Indian sacred spaces: sometimes the journey itself is the offering.

temples.name: Pashupatinath Temple
temples.essence: Where Shiva Looks in Eight Directions

body.p: Along the Shivna River in Mandsaur stands a remarkable form of Shiva: the rare Ashtamukhi, or eight-faced, Pashupatinath lingam. The dark stone image carries eight faces, each expressing a different manifestation of Shiva. Its unusual form immediately changes the way one experiences the deity. Shiva is no longer perceived through a single face or a single emotional quality. He appears as many aspects of the same divine consciousness.

The eight faces are traditionally associated with forms such as Bhava, Pashupati, Mahadeva, Ishana, Rudra, Sharva, Ugra and Ashani. Together, they suggest a Shiva who encompasses the gentle, the protective, the powerful, the terrifying and the cosmic. This multiplicity is central to the spiritual experience of the shrine. The devotee is reminded that the divine cannot always be reduced to one emotion.

The river beside the temple adds an especially beautiful layer to this symbolism. Water moves continuously, yet the stone image remains still. Devotion often works in the same way: life changes around us, but people seek a centre that does not move. Local tradition also connects the rising waters of the Shivna with the sacred image, making the river itself feel like a participant in the worship.

People come here seeking Shiva's protection, blessings and presence, but the deeper attraction is perhaps the sense of being seen from every direction. The eight-faced form can be experienced as a metaphor for the many dimensions of human life. There are parts of ourselves that are peaceful, parts that are fierce, parts that are wounded and parts that remain hidden. Shiva holds all of them.
At Pashupatinath, the sacred does not ask us to become only one version of ourselves. It reminds us that wholeness can contain many faces.

temples.name: Jatashankar
temples.essence: Where Shiva Hides Inside the Mountain

body.p: Deep within a natural cave near Pachmarhi, Shiva is worshipped in a landscape that feels older than the temple itself. Jatashankar is associated with naturally formed stone formations revered as lingams, with the cave's rock, darkness and water creating an atmosphere of profound inwardness. The name itself evokes Shiva's matted locks — jata — and the cave seems to embody that imagery through its tangled natural formations.

Regional tradition connects Jatashankar with the story of Shiva seeking refuge from Bhasmasura. Whether approached as sacred legend or as a symbolic story, the meaning is powerful: even Shiva, the great ascetic, can enter a hidden space. The cave therefore becomes a place associated with withdrawal, protection and silence.

For devotees, descending into Jatashankar can feel like leaving the ordinary world behind. Outside there is light, movement and the landscape of Pachmarhi. Inside, the senses change. The stone closes around the pilgrim, the air becomes cooler and the sound of water becomes more noticeable. The sacred is not presented through grandeur. It is encountered through darkness, rock and stillness.

This makes Jatashankar especially meaningful for people who are mentally exhausted or seeking a pause. Caves have always carried a powerful spiritual symbolism: they resemble the womb, the interior of the earth and the inward journey of consciousness. To enter one is, in a small way, to turn away from the external world and listen inward.
Jatashankar therefore feels less like a temple built inside nature and more like a temple that nature itself created.

temples.name: Kakanmath Temple
temples.essence: The Shiva Temple That Refuses to Disappear

body.p: In Sihoniya, the remains of Kakanmath rise dramatically from the landscape. The eleventh-century Shiva temple was built on a grand scale under the Kachchhapaghata rulers, and although much of the original complex has disappeared, the surviving structure still carries a striking sense of verticality and power. It is a temple in ruins, but not a ruin without presence.

There are places where broken stone feels like history. Kakanmath feels different. Its surviving walls, sculptural fragments and towering remains still create the impression of a sacred intention. The temple was dedicated to Shiva, the deity who in Indian thought is intimately connected with both creation and dissolution. Perhaps there is something fitting in seeing a Shiva temple endure through destruction: the deity of transformation inhabits a structure that has itself been transformed by time.

Local stories have attached unusual legends to the temple over the years, but beneath the legends is a simpler spiritual idea — devotion leaves traces. Kings disappear. Dynasties disappear. Buildings fall. Yet the desire to create a sacred centre can survive for centuries.

Standing before Kakanmath can therefore produce a very different emotion from visiting a perfectly restored temple. Instead of seeing only what remains, one begins imagining what once was: lamps, chants, bells, priests, offerings, festivals and generations of people who stood in almost the same place seeking Shiva.
The temple becomes a meditation on impermanence. What we build may not last forever. What we pray for may change. But the human impulse to search for something beyond the temporary continues.

temples.name: Bawangaja
temples.essence: Where the Mountain Becomes a Path to Liberation

body.p: On a hill in the Barwani region lies Bawangaja, an important Jain pilgrimage landscape known for its monumental image of Lord Adinath and its cluster of sacred shrines. The hill is not simply a place where a temple has been built. The ascent itself becomes part of the spiritual experience. The landscape encourages movement away from the ordinary and toward a quieter state of mind.

Jain spirituality places profound emphasis on self-discipline, non-attachment and liberation. In such a setting, the mountain becomes a natural metaphor for the soul's journey. One does not reach the higher point without effort. The climb asks for patience, while the stillness of the sacred landscape encourages contemplation.

Traditions associated with Bawangaja also connect the place with spiritual attainment and liberation. For devotees, such stories are not merely historical memories. They provide an emotional map: if others could walk the path toward release, then the path remains possible.

The great image of Adinath dominates the landscape, but the deeper experience is quieter than the monument itself. Jain sacred spaces often carry a particular stillness, because the central spiritual aspiration is not worldly victory but freedom from attachment. The visitor is invited to look inward rather than outward.
Bawangaja therefore adds another dimension to Madhya Pradesh's hidden sacred geography. Not every pilgrimage is about asking for something. Some are about learning to let something go.

temples.name: Shanka Shyamji
temples.essence: Where Krishna's Quiet Presence Meets the Hills

body.p: Away from the louder pilgrimage circuits of Madhya Pradesh, the Shanka Shyamji temple near Narsinghgarh carries the atmosphere of a quieter devotional tradition. Set amid the hills and landscapes around Narsinghgarh, the shrine is associated with Shyamji, a form of Krishna, and has long been connected with local faith and royal patronage.

There is a special quality to Krishna worship in places that remain relatively quiet. Krishna is often remembered through music, celebration, playfulness and the emotional language of bhakti. But in a secluded landscape, another side of that devotion appears — the intimate Krishna, the deity approached almost as a personal presence rather than as a distant cosmic figure.

The temple's setting reinforces this intimacy. The surrounding hills create a sense of distance from the speed of ordinary life, while the older architectural details carry traces of the community and rulers who sustained the shrine. This is not a temple that needs spectacle to create meaning. Its strength lies in continuity.

People are often drawn to Krishna not only for protection or blessings but for companionship. Bhakti allows the divine to be addressed with extraordinary emotional closeness — as beloved, friend, child or guide. In a quiet temple such as this, that relationship can feel especially personal.
Shanka Shyamji reminds us that some sacred places survive not because they dominate a landscape, but because they remain deeply loved by the people who return to them.

temples.name: Nemawar Siddheshwar
temples.essence: Where the Narmada Becomes a Pilgrim

body.p: At Nemawar, the Narmada becomes more than a river. It becomes part of the pilgrimage itself. The region has long been associated with sacred sites, Shiva worship and the spiritual culture of the Narmada, whose journey through Madhya Pradesh has inspired countless traditions of prayer, pilgrimage and renunciation.

The Siddheshwar tradition at Nemawar is rooted in the ancient Indian relationship between Shiva and sacred rivers. Shiva shrines beside the Narmada carry a particular emotional quality because the river is itself revered. The devotee is therefore not praying only within a temple. The entire landscape participates: water, stone, banks, sky and the rhythm of the river.

For people undertaking Narmada pilgrimage traditions, the river represents continuity. She flows through forests, villages, temples and cities, carrying the memory of countless generations. To stand beside her is to become briefly aware of a time scale much larger than one's own life.

Nemawar is therefore meaningful for those who seek grounding. Rivers have a way of making personal problems appear within a wider frame. What feels enormous in the mind can seem smaller beside a river that has been moving for centuries.

The sacredness of Nemawar lies in this relationship between movement and stillness. The Narmada keeps flowing. Shiva remains still. The pilgrim stands between them — carrying the concerns of a temporary life while looking toward something that feels eternal.
